summary: Introduces VLAN aggregation, a way to use IPv4 addresses more efficiently by sharing a subnet across several virtual LANs. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Instead of giving each small club a whole building of addresses, this lets many clubs share one building.

questions: how to share ip subnets across vlans
subtitle: Sharing an IP subnet across multiple virtual LANs to conserve address space

tldr.problem: Traditional IP addressing assigns a separate subnet to each virtual LAN, wasting address space on subnet overhead (network address, broadcast address, and a dedicated gateway) even for small deployments.
tldr.mechanism: VLAN aggregation allows multiple virtual LANs connected to the same physical switch to share a single IP subnet. Each VLAN becomes a separate broadcast domain but hosts are numbered from the shared subnet and use a common gateway address.
tldr.outcome: Networks conserve significant IPv4 address space, reduce administrative overhead, and gain flexibility in address allocation. The same IP subnet can support multiple customers or departments without requiring separate address blocks.

facts.label: Address conservation
facts.value: Traditional approach: 28 addresses for three customers; VLAN aggregation: 19 addresses

facts.label: Broadcast domain separation
facts.value: Each VLAN maintains separate Layer 2 broadcast domains

facts.label: Gateway sharing
facts.value: All sub-VLANs share a common default gateway address in the super-VLAN

facts.label: Initial deployments
facts.value: Extreme Networks in service provider data centers

today: RFC 3069 is an informational specification describing a technique for more efficient IP address allocation in switched networks. While the RFC has not been obsoleted, VLAN aggregation remains a specialized technique used primarily in service provider and large enterprise environments where address space conservation is critical.

sections.title: The Problem with Traditional Addressing
sections.content:
In a large switched network, each virtual LAN traditionally receives its own IP subnet. A subnet requires a network number, a broadcast address, and a gateway address, leaving only a small number of usable host addresses.

For example, a customer needing two hosts today but with projections for growth might be allocated a /28 subnet (16 addresses total), leaving only 13 usable addresses even though they need just 2. If another customer needs more addresses later, the entire subnet is allocated even though only a few addresses are used, and unused addresses cannot be reassigned to other customers within the same subnet.

When a customer's needs grow beyond the allocated subnet, renumbering becomes necessary, which can be costly and disruptive in production networks.
sections.eli5: Right now each group gets their own block of 16 or more addresses even if they only need 2, and you can't give the extra ones to another group.

sections.title: How VLAN Aggregation Works
sections.content:
VLAN aggregation introduces the concept of super-VLANs and sub-VLANs. Each customer's virtual LAN is a sub-VLAN that remains within a separate broadcast domain, preventing cross-VLAN communication at Layer 2. However, hosts on different sub-VLANs are numbered out of the same IP subnet (the super-VLAN subnet) and use the same default gateway address.

On the routed side of the network, the super-VLAN router performs Proxy ARP-like functions to enable communication between hosts on different sub-VLANs. This allows addressing to be much more efficient: instead of allocating separate /28, /29, and /30 subnets to three customers with different growth projections, all three are addressed from a single /24 subnet, using only the addresses they actually need.

If a customer needs additional addresses, they are simply allocated the next available address within the super-VLAN subnet, with no renumbering required.
sections.eli5: All groups share one big address pool (one subnet), each group gets its own quiet corner (broadcast domain), and a special router helps them talk to each other when needed.

sections.title: Implementation and Considerations
sections.content:
Extreme Networks has deployed VLAN aggregation in service provider data centers for over a year, demonstrating the technique in production environments. Other vendors are developing similar functionality.

One important consideration is directed broadcasts, which are framed at the Layer 2 broadcast domain level. The specification provides no support for directed broadcasts across the aggregated subnet, so <net, subnet, -1> directed broadcast addresses only apply to one Layer 2 broadcast domain.

For multicast traffic, the assumption is that the Layer 2 multicast domain matches the Layer 2 broadcast domain (the VLAN). IP multicast packets reaching all receivers in the IP subnet may require the multicast router to use IP host routes for the sender to perform correct Reverse Path Forwarding checks.
sections.eli5: This has been tested in real networks and works. But broadcast messages only go to one group, and multicast might need special setup.

sections.title: Security and Operational Safeguards
sections.content:
VLAN aggregation creates potential security vulnerabilities by allowing arbitrary allocation of addresses across disparate broadcast domains. The primary defense is to make address space ranges sticky: when an address or range is allocated to a specific sub-VLAN, the super-VLAN router should discard any IP or ARP packets received on that sub-VLAN with source addresses not allocated to it.

Implementation of these safeguards should remain local to the super-VLAN router, preventing interoperability issues with existing protocols. Logging and administrative alerting should occur when sticky-address violations are detected, enabling operators to identify unauthorized devices or misconfigurations.
sections.eli5: You need to make sure that if group A's router gets a packet claiming to be from group B's address, it throws the packet away and tells the network admin.
